confidence_note: Checked against the Williams translation and Stewart wording. Dropped from the old text: 'a good death is the reward of a good life', the claim that Seneca does not see retirement as a goal (he urges Paulinus to retire), and the invented daily practice. The 'live immediately' line (9.2) and the Stewart-style wording of 9.1 are medium confidence because translations vary.
facts: Augustus (4.2-4.5): never ceased to pray for rest and release from the affairs of state; in a letter he spoke of his deep desire for that time, long prayed for; he had shed blood by land and sea and plots formed in the city itself.

3.4-3.5: readers live as if they will live forever; the plan 'After my fiftieth year I'll retire to a life of leisure; my sixtieth year will bring release from all my duties'; answer: 'How late it is to begin living just when life must come to an end!'
5.2-5.3: Cicero wrote 'I'm lingering in my Tusculan estate, half-free'; the wise man will never be half-free but enjoy complete, unalloyed liberty.

9.1-9.2: 'The greatest impediment to living is expectancy, which relies on tomorrow and wastes today'; you arrange what is in Fortune's control and abandon what is in yours; the whole future lies in uncertainty, live immediately.

18-20: 'my dearest Paulinus' manages the revenues of the world and the public grain supply; Seneca urges him to withdraw to a more peaceful haven and calmer, safer, more important pursuits; such offices are bought at the cost of life; it is harder to obtain retirement from oneself than from the law; such men's funerals should be by torchlight and wax tapers, as if they had lived briefly.
scene_details: a letter in which the emperor writes of his long prayer for rest
the sentence 'After my fiftieth year I'll retire'
a funeral by torches and wax tapers
tension: The most powerful man in Rome and ordinary planners are all waiting for a later that may not come.
opening_idea: Open on the plan sentence, Augustus's letter, the expectancy line or Paulinus's grain office; each language its own.

lessons.idea: Give one postponed thing a place in this week.
lessons.anchor: Seneca names expectancy, relying on tomorrow, as the greatest impediment to living.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A baker who keeps promising her aunt a visit after the busy season writes it into the next free Sunday.

reflect_final: Which thing are you saving for after a busy stretch that you could begin in a small way this week?

use_cases.situation: The team keeps saying 'after the launch'.
use_cases.move: Cite the 'after my fiftieth year' plan and ask what can start small now.

use_cases.situation: You keep saying you will visit when things calm down.
use_cases.move: Pick a specific weekend and accept a short visit.

use_cases.situation: You are postponing something you care about.
use_cases.move: Put it in the next free calendar slot, small.

pocket_idea: Seneca named expectancy, living on tomorrow, the greatest impediment to living; move one 'later' into this week.
